content.comment_body: Hello, I'm preparing my program to use an [product_name] module for temperature comparison, though I don't have my PT100 sensor yet. My plan is to compare two temperatures using an analog comparator, but first I want to scale the input value. I understand that [company_name] converts the PT100 analog input into a digital value between 0 and 1000 in its internal register. I thought I could simply apply a gain of 0.25 and an offset of -50 to get a range from -50°C to 200°C with 0.25°C increments (0 gives -50°C, 1000 gives 200°C). Is it really this simple? Thanks for your guidance. My device is the latest version of [product_name].

Welcome to the forum. The analog-to-digital converter of [product_name] converts any analog signal (current, voltage, or PT100) into values from 0 to 1000 units. Even though it's a 10-bit converter, the scale is limited to 1000 instead of 1024 units. The [product_name] module is calibrated for a measuring range from -50°C to 200°C, which is a total span of 250°C. This means the resolution per unit is 250°C / 1000 = 0.25°C. Each increment represents a change of 0.25°C. You can display the converted value in three formats: without decimals (-50°C to 200°C), with one decimal (-50.0°C to 200.0°C), or with two decimals (-50.00°C to 200.00°C).

analysis.insight_summary: Users are looking for a straightforward explanation of how to scale and interpret analog input values when using an [product_name] module with PT100 sensors. The discussion clarifies that the analog signal is mapped to a range of 1000 units internally, and provides an accurate method for calculating the temperature resolution and mapping.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects the analog values from PT100 sensors to be mapped linearly, allowing for simple scaling using a gain and offset so temperatures are easily represented in digital form for logic programming.
pain_keywords: lack of PT100 sensor for testing
